title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent-Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and a single automated repair attempt—reduces unsafe network changes relative to LLM-only generation. In a preregistered paired design (N=500 intents run under both pipelines) we used gpt-5-mini for generation and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the adjudicating oracle. The GVR condition produced 500/500 accepted safe changes versus 496/500 for LLM-only (paired difference = 0.008; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.002, 0.016]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.125; preregistered per-test α = 0.025 after Bonferroni correction). Repairs were invoked only when the shared initial candidate failed the verifier: 4 repair calls in total (model calls = 504; mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008; median repair iterations under GVR = 0). The observed numerical advantage for GVR is small and does not meet the preregistered significance threshold. We (1) clarify the shared-initial generation protocol and reconcile execution accounting, (2) summarize the deterministic verifier's operational coverage and how 'safe' is defined, (3) document why the templated-automation confirmatory arm remains unexecuted in the archived run, (4) detail statistical methods and the small-discordance inference nuances, and (5) provide explicit pointers to the archived artifacts (execution/raw_results.jsonl; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv; execution/execution_manifest.json) that reconcile all reported numbers.

sections.introduction: Intent-driven automation for network configuration promises operational efficiency but risks outages and policy violations when generated changes are incorrect. Large language models (LLMs) can translate operator intent to device commands, but hallucination and sequencing errors reduce operational trust. Deterministic configuration verifiers can detect many correctness violations prior to deployment; combining generation with verification and automated repair (generate–verify–repair, GVR) is a plausible operational safeguard. Our preregistered research question: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → one automated repair attempt) yield a lower unsafe-change rate than LLM-only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? Contributions: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (N=500 intents) executed end-to-end with archived artifacts; (2) a concrete technical description reconciling shared-generation accounting and repair invocation; (3) transparent confirmatory statistics, detailed verifier coverage, and reproducibility pointers.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and systems research document active interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks including intent-to-configuration translation, AIOps, and multi-agent management frameworks. Prior work highlights hallucination and factual errors as central reliability concerns and proposes tool-augmented or verifier-assisted agents to mitigate those risks. Deterministic and formal configuration verification systems (e.g., Batfish-derived distributed verifiers and incremental checkers) provide operational oracles for reachability and policy constraints. However, the literature contains few preregistered, paired trials that quantitatively compare end-to-end generator-only pipelines versus verifier-augmented repair architectures on standardized NetOps change workloads. Our study is designed to fill that specific empirical gap within a bounded synthetic-task scope.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 before observing results. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Sampling: 500 distinct intents (paired), stratified 60% templateable / 40% complex across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Model and pipelines: generation used gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version). The experimental pipeline used a shared-initial-candidate protocol: for each intent the LLM produced one initial candidate configuration (shared_initial_generation) which was used for both arms to ensure strict pairing on generator output. Baseline (LLM-only) accepted the shared initial candidate without automated repair; guarded (GVR) applied the deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) to the same shared candidate and, if the verifier failed, invoked up to one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) per preregistration. The verifier's decision is the final adjudicating oracle for success/failure. Execution constraints: planned model-call budget = 1000; completed episodes = 1000 (500 pairs); model_calls_used = 504. Primary outcome: per-intent binary success = final accepted change passes deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Statistical analysis (pre-registered): exact paired-proportion test (exact McNemar two-sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CIs (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) over the 500 paired outcomes; multiplicity plan reserved a family α = 0.05 (two confirmatory comparisons) with Bonferroni per-test α = 0.025.
sections.results: Execution accounting and shared-initial protocol: the run produced 500 shared initial generator outputs (stage_count: shared_initial_generation = 500). Both conditions used the same shared candidate per intent. The guarded pipeline invoked the verifier on every shared candidate; repairs were requested only for verifier-failing cases and were therefore rare (repair stage_count = 4). This explains the apparent counting pattern: shared_initial_generation = 500 (one per intent), repair = 4 (only for the four verifier-failing initial candidates), and model_calls_used = 504 (500 initial + 4 repair calls). Baseline and guarded outcome counts (paired contingency): n11 = 496 (both succeed), n10 = 4 (guarded succeed, baseline fail), n01 = 0 (baseline succeed, guarded fail), n00 = 0 (both fail). Thus baseline success = 496/500 (0.992); guarded success = 500/500 (1.000); paired difference = 0.008. Statistical inference: exact McNemar two-sided test on discordant counts (n = n10 + n01 = 4, with k = n10 = 4 successes in the direction guarded>baseline) yields p = 0.125 (two-sided exact conditional binomial calculation; the analysis record lists test = exact_mcnemar_two_sided, p_value = 0.125). Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. Reconciling CI and p-value: the bootstrap CI is a confidence interval for the paired difference distribution under resampling of pairs and excludes zero by a small margin; the exact McNemar p-value tests a discrete null of symmetry in discordant counts and is conservative when discordant counts are small and all in one direction (here n = 4, k = 4 → two-sided exact p = 0.125). Under the preregistered per-test α = 0.025 (Bonferroni), the observed p = 0.125 is not significant. Exploratory diagnostics and costs: only 4 repair calls were invoked across 500 guarded tasks; total model calls = 504; mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 1.008; median repair iterations under GVR = 0. Missingness, contamination, and reconciliation: complete_pair_count = 500; no technical failures recorded; all reported primary numbers reconcile deterministically with archived artifacts (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/raw_results.jsonl).
sections.discussion: Operational meaning: In this synthetic workload the GVR pipeline eliminated the four verifier-detected unsafe initial candidates that the LLM-only arm would have accepted, at minimal model-call overhead. The numerical improvement is small (0.8 percentage points) and did not meet the preregistered significance threshold after multiplicity adjustment. Important caveats and threats to validity: (1) construct validity—'safe' is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5's checks (see verifier specification below); verifier blind spots imply that passing the verifier is necessary but not sufficient for all real-world safety properties; (2) external validity—tasks were synthetic topology profiles and vendor-agnostic CLI abstractions; production hardware, vendor-specific CLIs, and live telemetry were not evaluated; (3) model scope—only gpt-5-mini was evaluated; multi-model generality is untested; (4) unexecuted preregistered arm—the templated-automation comparator was preregistered but not executed in this archived run (see Deviations paragraph below); (5) inferential power—the preregistration targeted an absolute paired increase of ≈8 percentage points for power calculations; the observed effect (0.8 percentage points) is an order of magnitude smaller, so the study was not powered to treat such a small effect as definitive. Practical implication: where even rare unsafe changes are unacceptable, integrating deterministic verification and an automated repair step can reduce accepted unsafe changes with modest cost—subject to verifier coverage limitations.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment (N=500), a generate–verify–repair pipeline using gpt-5-mini plus deterministic_netops_validator_v5 produced numerically fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM-only generation (500 vs 496 safe outcomes). The paired difference (0.008) favors GVR but does not meet the preregistered per-test significance threshold after multiplicity correction (exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.125; 95% bootstrap CI [0.002, 0.016]). Repairs were invoked only when the shared initial candidate failed verification (4 repair calls total), so overhead was negligible in this run. We recommend broader replication with multiple LLMs, more comprehensive verifiers, adversarial NetOps-tailored robustness evaluation, and execution of the preregistered templated-automation arm before asserting production readiness. All primary artifacts and reconciliation files are archived and referenced below for reproducibility.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The declared generation model in the archived run is 'gpt-5-mini' (execution/model_configuration.json). The orchestration adapter family was 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1' using the hosted provider 'openai_responses'. Key automated components recorded in the archived run: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (task synthesis), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (primary deterministic verifier/scorer), and the GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus an automated single-repair step (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The study preregistration is study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29 and the preregistration manifest SHA-256 archived with the run is aa8982a27c73e51521ac023a78adcfa358ef3978c0f9bc05213801fcbd2f1d0a. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at 'provenance/master_prompt.txt' with SHA-256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and Large Language Models for NetOps) prior to the autonomy lock; all literature search, study-selection, experiment design, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, peer review, and revision were performed autonomously after the lock. No human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock. The execution completed without recorded technical deviations in the embedded execution manifest; all primary artifacts, logs, and reconciliations are archived in the evidence bundle and the full hash manifest is available at execution/execution_manifest.json within the bundle.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor-specific CLIs, and live telemetry is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi-model generality is not established.

Safety is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5's coverage: the verifier enforces syntactic parsing, required-sequence/workflow-policy checks (protected interfaces, must_be_down_for_fields, group constraints), dependency-rule enforcement, and final-state comparison to the task's expected_final_state. Violation codes mark specific rule breaches; any non-empty violation set yields a failing verdict. Verifier blind spots remain a limitation—passing the verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks not encoded in its checks.

The preregistered templated-automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run. No post-lock deviation record appears in the archived deviation log; therefore the templated comparison remains unexecuted and the second confirmatory test listed in the preregistration is unresolved in this dataset. As a result, the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) was only partially applicable to executed comparisons; the reported p-value and CI are those for the executed GVR vs LLM-only comparison and are compared against the preregistered per-test α as described.
Replicated adversarial robustness against NetOps-targeted prompt injection or maliciously crafted inputs was not evaluated and remains future work.
